title: Arjuna Sees Only the Bird
hook: Drona asks his students what they see, and only Arjuna sees just the bird: Vaisheshika's mind, one gate at a time
carry: the mind is one gate; the self is the knower
tomorrow: why does a flame always rise? Vaisheshika's answer goes back to dharma.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhrigu's kick and Vaisheshika's six kinds of thing: the person, the passing mood, the act that's over. Today closes a week.
screen: `MEET THE PERSON, NOT THE KICK.` · `THE WEEK CLOSES.`

segments.voice: Drona, teacher of the Kuru princes, has a wooden bird set high in a tree. One by one he calls his students up, bows drawn. What do you see? Yudhishthira says: the tree, the bird, you, my brothers. Step aside, says Drona. The others say much the same. Then Arjuna. What do you see? Only the bird. Describe it. I see its head, nothing else. Shoot, says Drona. And the head falls.
screen: `WHAT DO YOU SEE?` → `THE TREE, YOU, MY BROTHERS.` → `ONLY ITS HEAD.`

segments.voice: That's the Mahabharata; popular retellings make it the bird's eye. Vaisheshika gives you a way to see what happened. Its first category, substance, comes in nine kinds. Earth, water, fire, air: the four kinds of atom. Then akasha, the space that carries sound. Then time and direction. And last, two that aren't stuff at all: the self, atman, and the mind, manas. How do you know there's a self? The Sutra lists its marks, and the first is breathing out and breathing in. Then the eyelids opening and closing, life itself, and further on, pleasure, pain, desire, aversion and effort. And the mind? Sometimes, the Sutra notes, self, senses and object are all in contact, and still no knowing happens. You stare at a page and take nothing in. Something has to be the gate, and that gate is manas. In this school it's tiny, so it joins one sense at a time. On this view, nobody truly reads and listens at once; the mind only switches, fast. Read Arjuna that way: his eyes took in the whole tree like everyone's, but his mind let in only the bird. Hindu practice prizes that one-pointed mind, ekagrata, and trains it with one bead, one name, one flame. Behind the gate is the self, the knower. So the week closes: Gargi's honest questions, the voice that only sounded like Rama, Nachiketa's doubt, the gleaner's handful, the seed, Bhrigu's kick, and now the bird. At a desk with three screens open, the old school's line holds: one gate, one thing.
screen: `NINE SUBSTANCES.` · `BREATH IS A SIGN OF THE SELF.` · `THE MIND: ONE THING AT A TIME.` · `ARJUNA SEES ONLY THE BIRD.` · then, large: `ONE GATE, ONE THING.`

segments.voice: Take a mala if you have one, or just use your fingers. With each bead or each finger, say one name of God, Om, Ram, Shiva, whichever is yours. If you don't pray, count one breath. One bead, one name. When a sound pulls you away, that's the gate swinging; swing it back. Like Arjuna: only the bird.
Vaisheshika. Its nine substances end with the self, known by signs like breathing, and the mind, a gate that lets in one thing at a time.
Your line: the mind is one gate; the self is the knower. Arjuna saw only the bird. A week of two schools, done.

howItsDone: Students of Vaisheshika learn the nine substances, from earth to mind, and the Nyaya-Vaisheshika tradition uses the self's marks to argue that the self is real; in Hindu practice, japa on a mala, one bead and one name at a time, trains the same one-pointed mind.

what a scholar hears: Vaisheshika Sutra 3.2.1 gives the mark of manas as the arising or non-arising of knowledge; 3.2.4 lists breathing and the rest as marks of the self; Drona's bird test is in the Mahabharata's Adi Parva.
